sections.title: Migration went the other way first
sections.intro: Before European politics worried about Africans arriving, European projects treated Africa as land for Europe's emigrants, and African labour as something to be taken or forced.

facts.text: In the 1920s and 1930s the Pan-European movement cast Africa as 'Europe's plantation' and as the answer to Europe's own 'overpopulation': Europeans, not Africans, were to emigrate.
In 1929 Richard Coudenhove-Kalergi wrote that Africa could give Europe 'land for its overpopulation, labour for its unemployed'.
The same writer warned that Europe must at all costs prevent 'great numbers of black workers and soldiers' from immigrating to Europe.
Fascist Italy promoted 'demographic imperialism': moving large numbers of unemployed Italians to Libya, Ethiopia and Eritrea.
Today Spain's enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla serve, in the authors' words, as hubs in the EU's 'militarized quest to control migration from Africa'.
At the Cape, the Dutch East India Company (VOC) imported about 63,000 enslaved people from Asia and other parts of Africa between 1652 and 1808.
The first enslaved people were brought to the Cape as Company labourers, for building the fort, fishing, saltworks, brickmaking and domestic work.

sections.title: Who moves, and where to
sections.intro: Most Africans who leave their country do not go to Europe. They move to a neighbouring country, often within the same region.

facts.text: In 2024, about 25.1 million African migrants lived in another African country, 17.4% more than the 20.7 million Africans living outside the continent (SWP analysis of UN DESA International Migrant Stock 2024).

Of the 20.7 million African migrants living outside Africa in 2024, 10.6 million were in Europe (geographic Europe, not only the EU), 6.7 million in Asia, 2.7 million in North America, 0.6 million in Oceania and 0.06 million in Latin America and the Caribbean (SWP, from UN DESA data).
The number of African migrants living outside the continent grew only modestly, from 19.7 million in 2020 to 20.7 million in 2024 (SWP, from UN DESA data).
In 2024 about 3% of Africa's population were international migrants (SWP, from UN DESA data).
Around 55% of African migrants living in European countries in 2024 came from Northern Africa (5.8 million) (SWP, from UN DESA data).
In 2020, by the Mo Ibrahim Foundation's reading of UN DESA data, 51.6% of African migrants lived within Africa and 27.2% lived in Europe.

Counts differ slightly by source and year: the IOM-African Union Africa Migration Report (2024), using UN DESA 2020 data, counts 20.8 million intra-African migrants against 19.7 million Africans living outside Africa and 4.3 million non-Africans living in Africa, a narrower margin than SWP's 25.1 million versus 20.7 million for 2024; both find a majority stay on the continent.

The IOM-AU Africa Migration Report (2024) notes North Africa is the exception: emigrants from Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia mostly live in Europe, while those from Egypt and Sudan mostly went to Middle Eastern countries.

In 2020, 63% of all migrants born in sub-Saharan Africa lived in another country of sub-Saharan Africa, which UN DESA says contradicts the common perception that Europe is the main destination of African migration; about one third of that intra-regional migration was refugees and asylum seekers.

Migration researchers Flahaux and de Haas argue that emigration out of Africa is increasing mainly from the relatively more developed African countries, because higher income, education and access to information increase people's capabilities and aspirations to migrate (N-IUSSP, 2016).
On 1 January 2025, 46.7 million people born outside the EU lived in the EU-27, 10.4% of its 450.6 million residents (Eurostat; this counts all non-EU countries of birth, not only Africa).
On 1 January 2025, Moroccans were the third-largest group of non-EU citizens living in the EU-27, after Ukrainians and Turks (Eurostat).
In 2025, refugees in the EU were 1.9% of its total population, and the European Commission notes that most refugees from Africa and Asia move to neighbouring countries rather than to Europe.
At end-2024, almost 87% of African refugees and asylum seekers (10.6 million) were hosted in Africa and 13% (1.6 million) outside it (SWP calculations from UNHCR data).

At end-2025, the largest refugee-hosting countries worldwide were Colombia (2.8 million), Germany (2.7 million), Türkiye (2.4 million), Uganda (1.9 million), Iran (1.7 million), Chad (1.5 million) and Pakistan (1.3 million) (UNHCR; refugees and other people in need of international protection).
Uganda hosted 1.9 million refugees at end-2025, about 1 million of them from South Sudan and 644,500 from the DR Congo; Chad hosted 1.5 million, nine in ten of them Sudanese (UNHCR).
By end-2025 refugees from Sudan numbered 2.8 million, hosted mostly in neighbouring countries: Chad (1.3 million), South Sudan (571,100) and Libya (551,700) (UNHCR).

At end-2025, 65% of the world's refugees were hosted in neighbouring countries; low-income countries, with 8% of world population and 0.3% of global GDP, hosted 18% of refugees, including very large populations in Chad, DR Congo, South Sudan, Sudan and Uganda (UNHCR).

At end-2025, UNHCR counted 22.7 million forcibly displaced people in countries of its Eastern and Southern Africa region and 16.4 million in West and Central Africa, against 18.1 million in its Europe region.

Around 31.7 million people were living in internal displacement in sub-Saharan Africa at end-2025, almost 39% of the global total of 82.2 million; it was the region's first decline in at least a decade, mostly due to returns in DR Congo and Sudan (IDMC).

Sub-Saharan Africa recorded 17.3 million internal displacements (movements) in 2025, 14.5 million (83%) triggered by conflict and violence; DR Congo alone recorded over 9.7 million conflict displacements (IDMC).
In Sudan, 9.1 million people remained internally displaced at end-2025 despite the first reported returns since the war began (IDMC).

sections.title: What people flee
sections.intro: War, persecution, forced service without end, and disasters drive most of the displacement. Europe's own asylum offices accept most claims from some of these countries.

facts.text: By February 2025, nearly two years of war in Sudan had displaced about 12 million people inside the country and across its borders, roughly one-third of the population, according to OCHA and UNHCR.
As of February 2025, nearly 3.5 million people had fled Sudan to neighbouring countries (UN plan covering the Central African Republic, Chad, Egypt, Ethiopia, Libya, South Sudan and Uganda).

IOM said in April 2026 that at the height of the Sudan war nearly 12 million people fled, more than 4.5 million crossed into neighbouring countries (above all Egypt, South Sudan and Chad), and almost nine million remained internally displaced.

By April 2026 nearly four million displaced Sudanese had returned to their places of origin, IOM said, some because they believed security had improved and others because life in displacement had become unbearable.
IDMC counted about 9.1 million internally displaced people in Sudan at the end of 2025, 62 per cent of them in Darfur.

In February 2026 the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan reported that the RSF operation in and around El Fasher bore the defining characteristics of genocide, finding at least three of the five genocidal acts met (as reported by Al Jazeera).
The UN Special Rapporteur on Eritrea reported in 2025 (period April 2024–April 2025) that indefinite national service affected every aspect of life and continued to push thousands to flee.
According to the same 2025 UN report, most Eritreans are forced to serve in national service for periods from several years to more than two decades.

As at June 2024, over 683,000 Eritreans, 18 per cent of the population, had fled the country according to UNHCR figures cited by the UN Special Rapporteur, making Eritrea the tenth-largest origin of refugees and asylum-seekers globally.
In 2016 the UN Commission of Inquiry on Eritrea found reasonable grounds to believe that crimes against humanity, including enslavement, had been committed in Eritrea since 1991.

Not every European authority treats Eritrean conscription as grounds for protection: in 2018 a Swiss court ruled that rejected Eritrean asylum seekers could be deported even if they risked being called up for national service.
In 2025 EU+ asylum authorities granted protection at first instance to 76% of Eritreans and 70% of Sudanese, with high rates across most EU+ countries (EUAA).
The EU+ first-instance recognition rate for Malians was 84% in both 2024 and 2025 and rose to 87% in the first half of 2026 (EUAA).
By contrast, some North African nationalities had very low EU+ recognition rates in 2025: Moroccans 4% and Egyptians 3% (EUAA).

Outcomes vary by receiving country: in 2025 Malians' first-instance recognition rates ranged from close to 100% in some EU+ countries to around 10% in others, and Somalis' from around 20-30% in some countries to over 90% in others (EUAA).

EUAA, which counts only refugee status and subsidiary protection, put the EU+ first-instance recognition rate at 29% in 2025, the lowest on record, so headline rates depend on what is counted as protection.
Eurostat, which counts national humanitarian status as well as refugee status and subsidiary protection, put the EU-27 first-instance recognition rate at 39.1% in 2025.

EUAA notes that applicants from Somalia, among others, are often given national rather than international protection, which its 2025 statistics record as negative decisions, so the published rate understates how many are allowed to stay.

About 4 million people were displaced across Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger and neighbouring countries in October 2025, around two-thirds more than five years earlier, driven by insecurity, lack of services and livelihoods, and climate change (UNHCR).

UNHCR reported in October 2025 that displaced young people in the central Sahel face forced recruitment, trafficking and limited job opportunities, raising the risk of dangerous journeys beyond the region.

The central Sahel hosted nearly three million internally displaced people (about two million in Burkina Faso, 548,000 in Niger and 415,000 in Mali), plus about one million refugees in neighbouring countries, per UNHCR figures cited by UNRIC in May 2026.

Sub-Saharan Africa recorded 17.3 million internal displacements in 2025, 14.5 million (83%) of them caused by conflict and violence, and 31.7 million people were living in internal displacement at year-end (IDMC).

In eastern DR Congo, over 9.7 million conflict displacements were recorded in 2025, nearly twice the 2024 record, as M23 seized major cities; 4.3 million people remained displaced by conflict at year-end (IDMC).
Nigeria had 3.5 million internally displaced people at the end of 2025, nearly half of them in the north-eastern state of Borno (IDMC).

Somalia's 2022 drought, the longest and most severe in 40 years, triggered a record 1.1 million internal displacements; most people moved within their own region seeking security, livelihoods and aid (IDMC).
Human Rights Watch reported in May 2025 that since Uganda's Anti-Homosexuality Act was enacted on 26 May 2023, authorities had arbitrarily arrested, entrapped and extorted LGBT people.

Not everyone flees war or persecution: in UNDP's 2019 survey of irregular African migrants in Europe, 58% had been earning (49%) or in school (9%) when they left, and for 66% of those earning, income did not hold them back from migrating.
The same UNDP survey found that 62% of respondents felt they had been treated unfairly by their governments, showing economic and political motives often overlap.

In a Mixed Migration Centre survey of 531 refugees and migrants who passed through Tunisia (interviews July–October 2024), 76% cited economic reasons for leaving and 62% conflict or insecurity, with most giving more than one reason.

sections.title: Routes, smugglers and traffickers
sections.intro: Smuggling is a paid crossing; trafficking is exploitation by force, fraud or coercion. On the routes to Europe the two often meet, and people die on the way.

facts.text: Under the 2000 UN Smuggling of Migrants Protocol, migrant smuggling means procuring, for a financial or other material benefit, someone's illegal entry into a country where they are not a national or permanent resident: in other words, a paid service to cross a border irregularly.

Under the 2000 UN Trafficking in Persons Protocol, trafficking means moving or holding people by force, coercion, abduction, fraud, deception or abuse of vulnerability for the purpose of exploitation, and a victim's consent is irrelevant once any of those means is used.
The Smuggling Protocol (Article 5) states that migrants must not be criminally prosecuted under it for having been smuggled.

In 2023 Frontex detected around 158,000 irregular crossings on the Central Mediterranean route (up 50% on 2022) and over 40,000 on the Western African route to the Canary Islands, then its highest annual figure; Frontex notes the same person may be counted more than once.

In 2024 Central Mediterranean crossings fell 59% to about 67,000 because of fewer departures from Tunisia and Libya, while Canary Islands arrivals rose 18% to almost 47,000, the highest since Frontex began collecting data in 2009, driven by departures from Mauritania (EU external borders, preliminary data).

In 2025 irregular border crossings detected at the EU's external borders fell 26% to almost 178,000; the Central Mediterranean stayed the most active route at about the 2024 level, the Western Africa route fell by around two-thirds, and the Western Mediterranean rose, mainly through departures from Algeria.

Italy's Interior Ministry recorded 157,651 sea arrivals in 2023, 66,617 in 2024 and 66,296 in 2025 (provisional, subject to consolidation); in 2025 the most common declared nationality at landing was Bangladeshi (20,164), followed by Egyptian (9,091) and Eritrean (7,579).

Spain's Interior Ministry reported 36,775 irregular arrivals in 2025, down 42.6% from 64,019 in 2024; arrivals in the Canary Islands fell 62% to 17,788, while Balearic Islands arrivals, mainly from Algeria, rose 24.5% to 7,321 (as reported by AFP).

The fall in Atlantic departures followed a 2024 EU–Mauritania pact (210 million euros) to curb crossings; Human Rights Watch reported in August 2025 systematic abuses of migrants by Mauritanian border personnel, including rape, torture and extortion, which Mauritania rejects.
IOM estimates cited by Frontex put deaths in the Mediterranean at at least 2,573 in 2024 and at least 1,878 in 2025.
IOM's Missing Migrants Project recorded at least 3,129 deaths and disappearances in the Mediterranean in 2023, the highest since 2017 (reported by AFP).

For 2025 IOM recorded some 3,400 deaths and disappearances on sea routes to Europe, including 1,330 on the Central Mediterranean and more than 1,200 on the Western Africa/Atlantic route to the Canary Islands; IOM says aid cuts and restricted information made more missing migrants invisible.
IOM recorded 7,904 deaths and disappearances on migration routes worldwide in 2025, down from a record 9,200 in 2024, and says its figures represent only the lowest boundary of the true number.

Counts of deaths differ by method: while IOM documents a minimum, the Spanish NGO Caminando Fronteras, which compiles reports from families and rescue statistics, counted over 3,000 deaths on routes to Spain in 2025, far above IOM's figure of more than 1,200 for the Atlantic route.

A joint UNHCR–IOM–Mixed Migration Centre report (2024) found 1,180 people known to have died crossing the Sahara between January 2020 and May 2024, with the real number believed much higher; deaths in the desert are presumed to be double those at sea, against about 7,115 dead or missing in the Mediterranean in the same period.

The UN Independent Fact-Finding Mission on Libya (March 2023) found crimes against humanity committed against migrants in places of detention controlled by Libya's Directorate for Combating Illegal Migration, the Libyan Coast Guard and the Stability Support Apparatus, entities that received EU and member-state support.

The Mission (2023) found that guards demanded payment to release migrants and that trafficking, enslavement, forced labour, extortion and smuggling generated significant revenue for individuals, groups and state institutions; it also found overwhelming evidence of systematic torture in detention.

The Mission (2023) described a cycle in which migrants entering Libya, often with smugglers, are captured, recaptured and transferred between official and unofficial detention places without judicial review; it counted more than 670,000 migrants from over 41 countries in Libya.

UNODC estimates that in 2023, 254,422 people departed North Africa on the Central Mediterranean route but 150,653 were registered as arriving in Europe, and that 77–93% of those leaving Libya and 66–89% of those leaving Tunisia were smuggled.

UNODC estimates smugglers charged on average about US$1,171 for a sea crossing from Tunisia and between US$850 and US$4,500 from Libya depending on nationality, putting the 2023 Central Mediterranean sea-smuggling market at US$290–370 million.

For 2025 UNODC estimated that 190,000–209,000 people were smuggled on four main sea routes to Europe, earning smugglers US$388–509 million, with IOM-reported fees from US$170 for the Canary Islands crossing to over US$7,500 towards Italy and Malta (as reported by OCCRP).

UNODC (2024) finds no single group dominates smuggling on the Central and Western Mediterranean routes, but a variety of actors with different levels of organisation, plus some self-organised departures from Tunisia and Morocco; smuggling is linked to corruption from border checkpoints to senior government levels.

UNODC (2024) reports that on the Central and Western Mediterranean routes many migrants are smuggled only to end up trafficked for sexual or labour exploitation, including at artisanal gold-mining sites in West and Central Africa.
UNODC (2024) notes that smuggled migrants who cannot pay are sometimes coerced into steering boats or other roles as payment, so that they, rather than the organisers, bear the risk if intercepted.

Research disagrees on whether sea rescue draws more crossings: a 2023 Scientific Reports study of the Central Mediterranean found that Libyan pushbacks affected flows but search-and-rescue periods did not, finding no support for rescue as a driver of irregular migration.

By contrast, a 2024 study in the American Economic Journal: Economic Policy found that after rescue operations intensified in 2013 smugglers sent boats in worse weather and on flimsier rafts, offsetting safety gains; the authors still judged rescue likely raised migrant welfare and recommended restricting raft supply and expanding legal alternatives.

sections.title: "They take our jobs": what research finds
sections.intro: Most studies find small or no effects on the wages and jobs of people born in the country, and some find losses for specific groups. Europe also has jobs it cannot fill.

facts.text: In the second quarter of 2026 the job vacancy rate was 2.1% in the euro area and 2.0% in the EU-27, slightly down from a year earlier (EU: 2.1% in Q2 2025): the labour market is cooling but vacancies persist.

In Q2 2026 the highest job vacancy rates in the EU were in the Netherlands (4.1%); Italy's rate (whole economy, not strictly comparable because the public sector is not surveyed) was 1.5%, down 0.3 points on Q2 2025.

Across the 31 EURES countries in 2024, the most widespread shortage occupations, reported in at least 75% of countries, were welders, nursing professionals, cooks and building electricians; the most acute were heavy truck drivers, specialist doctors and nurses.
The European Labour Authority's 2024 report found Italy among the countries reporting the highest labour shortages, alongside Malta, Slovakia, Bulgaria and Romania.

Eurostat's EUROPOP2025 projections show the EU working-age population (20-64) falling from 58.3% of the population (263.2 million) in 2025 to 49.7% (198.4 million) in 2100, a loss of 64.9 million people.

ISTAT projects (median scenario, base 2025) that the share of Italy's residents aged 15-64 will fall from 63.4% to 55.3% by 2050, and the 15-64 labour force from 24.8 to 21.4 million, about 3.4 million fewer.
ISTAT expects Italy's net international migration to stay positive but too small to offset the persistent excess of deaths over births (projections base 1 January 2025).
Fondazione Leone Moressa, citing Unioncamere-Excelsior estimates, reports that Italy will need about 3.7 million workers in 2025-2029, largely to replace people retiring.
David Card (1990) found that the 1980 Mariel boatlift raised Miami's labour force by 7% yet appeared to have had virtually no effect on the wages or unemployment of less-skilled workers.
George Borjas's reappraisal (2015 working paper, published 2017) argued that, looking only at high-school dropouts, Mariel lowered their wages in Miami by 10 to 30 percent.

Peri and Yasenov, re-examining Mariel with a synthetic control method, found no significant wage difference for non-Cuban high-school dropouts in Miami after 1980, and attributed Borjas's large effects to measurement error in small samples.

Using Danish data for 1991-2008 and a refugee dispersal policy, Foged and Peri found that inflows of refugee-country immigrants pushed low-educated Danish workers into less manual jobs, with positive effects on their wages, employment and mobility.

A study of a policy that let Czech workers commute to German border areas (Dustmann, Schönberg and Stuhler, 2016) found a moderate fall in local native wages and a sharp fall in local native employment, driven mainly by fewer natives entering work.

A Bank of Italy study using EU Labour Force Survey data for 1996-2010 (D'Amuri and Peri) found that more immigrants pushed native workers toward more complex tasks without reducing the total number of jobs available to them; doubling immigrant numbers was associated with 0.7% higher average wages.
For Spain, Carrasco, Jimeno and Ortega (census and work-permit data, 1991-2001) found no significant effect of immigration on Spanish workers' employment rate or wages.

The OECD found that in the 25 OECD countries studied, on average over 2006-2018, immigrants paid more in taxes and contributions than governments spent on their social protection, health and education.

The same OECD study found immigrants' total net fiscal contribution was small, between -1% and +1% of GDP in most countries in 2006-2018, with differences largely due to the age of migrant populations.

Fondazione Leone Moressa estimates that foreign residents in Italy produced a net fiscal balance of +1.0 billion euros (45 billion in revenue against 44 billion in spending), and that over 5 million foreign-born taxpayers paid 12.6 billion euros in income tax (Irpef).

In 2025 foreign citizens made up 10.7% of Italy's employed (about 2.6 million) and produced 9.7% of value added (197 billion euros), with higher shares in agriculture (21.3%), construction (18.4%) and restaurants (14.4%), according to Fondazione Leone Moressa on ISTAT data.
Foreign workers in Italy are concentrated in low-skilled work: in 2025 about 30% of employed foreign citizens held unskilled jobs, almost four times the 8% among Italians.
Italy's 2026-2028 'decreto flussi' sets quotas for 497,550 non-EU workers (164,850 in 2026), for seasonal and non-seasonal employment and self-employment.

Few quota places become legal jobs: according to the Ero Straniero campaign's report, only 14,349 residence permits were issued in 2025 against 181,450 planned entries (7.9%), and 24,858 against 146,850 in 2024.

The FLAI-CGIL Placido Rizzotto Observatory (2024 report) notes that ISTAT counts about 200,000 irregular workers in Italian agriculture, with an irregularity rate of 30% for employees, and argues field research shows this is an underestimate.

Over 2015-2022 about 2.4 million people held agricultural employee contracts in Italy, about 900,000 of them foreign (over a third); the median annual pay per worker was just over 6,000 euros (2024 Agromafie report on INPS data).

Al Jazeera reported in 2024 on African workers in Piedmont's Langhe vineyards, such as a Gambian man recruited by a gangmaster (caporale) who worked 12-hour shifts for 3-4 euros an hour without a contract or legal status.

Italy's National Action Plan against labour exploitation in agriculture, developed with ILO and EU support, builds on Law 199 of 2016 on caporalato and rests on four pillars: prevention, protection, enforcement and remedies.

sections.title: What Europe pays, and what it receives
sections.intro: Most people who come to the EU from outside arrive with a permit. The EU also pays transit countries to stop departures, and the people who left send money home.

facts.text: The EU Emergency Trust Fund for Africa (EUTF), set up in 2015 with an initial €1.8 billion, had received more than €5 billion in contributions, most of it (€4.4 billion, 88%) from the European Development Fund and the EU budget, according to the European Court of Auditors in 2024.
By the end of 2023 the EUTF, active in 27 countries across the Sahel and Lake Chad, the Horn of Africa and North Africa, had paid out €4.508 billion of its €5 billion endowment.

The European Court of Auditors concluded in 2024 that EUTF support 'remained insufficiently focused', spread across too wide a range of development, humanitarian and security actions, and that human rights risks were not comprehensively addressed.
The Court of Auditors found in 2024 that there was insufficient data to show the EUTF's impact, in particular on reducing the number of migrants using the Central Mediterranean route.

Assessing EUTF projects in Libya, the Court of Auditors (2024) noted that EUTF support may have facilitated the transfer of migrants to detention centres, worsening overcrowding, and that the Commission had no formal procedure for following up allegations of human rights violations.

Italy and Libya signed a Memorandum of Understanding on 2 February 2017; together with the EU's Malta Declaration a day later it became the basis for EU-funded support (speedboats, a coordination centre, training) to the Libyan coast guard.

In 2021 the Libyan coast guard, supported by Italy and the EU, intercepted 32,425 refugees and migrants at sea and returned them to Libya, by Amnesty International's count the highest figure on record.

Human Rights Watch estimated in February 2023 that around 108,000 people had been returned to Libya since the 2017 deal, while only about 9,000 refugees had been evacuated by UNHCR's emergency mechanism in the same period.

In March 2023 the UN Independent Fact-Finding Mission on Libya found that crimes against humanity had been committed against migrants in detention, and that the entities involved had received technical, logistical and financial support from the EU and its member states to intercept migrants.

A member of the UN Libya mission said in 2023 that the EU and its member states were not found responsible for the crimes themselves, but that their support 'has aided and abetted the commission of the crimes'.
The Court of Auditors reported in 2024 that the Libyan Coast Guard, the main Libyan actor at sea, received its first EUTF-funded boat in June 2023.

The EU-Tunisia memorandum of July 2023 earmarked an initial €105 million for migration (anti-smuggling, border management and faster returns of rejected asylum seekers) and around €150 million in budget support; the text itself was vague on figures.

Hours before the EU-Tunisia deal was announced in July 2023, AFP reporters at the Tunisia-Libya border saw dozens of exhausted migrants in the desert who said Tunisian authorities had taken them there.

In October 2024 the European Ombudsman criticised the Commission for publishing nothing about the human rights risk assessment behind the 2023 Tunisia MoU, and asked it to publish clear criteria for suspending EU funding over human rights violations.

In March 2024 the EU signed a €7.4 billion partnership with Egypt (including €5 billion in concessional loans and €200 million for migration management), far larger than its deals with Tunisia (€700 million) and Mauritania (€210 million).

Of the €210 million in the EU-Mauritania migration partnership (2024), €100 million is described as general budget support, with the rest covering border surveillance, anti-smuggling, search and rescue and support to Malian refugees, according to Statewatch's monitoring of EU documents.

In 2025 the EU-27 issued about 3.9 million first residence permits to non-EU citizens, the highest since records began in 2008; 33.6% were for employment, 28.1% for family, 15.5% for education and 22.8% for other reasons including international protection.
Moroccans were the third-largest group receiving first residence permits in the EU in 2025 (202,054, 5.2% of the total), and family was the main reason for their permits (47.9%).

Frontex detected almost 178,000 irregular border crossings at the EU's external borders in 2025 (all nationalities, detections rather than individuals), down 26% on 2024 and less than half the 2023 total.

In 2025 the Central Mediterranean remained the busiest route into the EU at about 2024 levels, while detections on the Western Africa (Atlantic) route fell by around two-thirds, driven by fewer departures from Mauritania, Morocco and Senegal.

Across all routes in 2025 the most frequently detected nationalities were Bangladeshis, Egyptians and Afghans; IOM estimated that at least 1,878 people died in the Mediterranean in 2025, against 2,573 in 2024.
Remittances to Sub-Saharan Africa reached $54 billion in 2023 (a 0.3% fall), nearly 1.5 times the region's FDI inflows of $38.6 billion, and were more stable than FDI.
The World Bank noted in 2024 that Sub-Saharan Africa faced a funding squeeze made worse by falling ODA relative to GDP, and that the region had the world's highest costs for sending remittances.
In 2023 remittances made up more than a fifth of GDP in the Gambia, Lesotho and Comoros.
For the Middle East and North Africa region (which includes Egypt, Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia as well as non-African countries), remittances in 2023 were more than twice the sum of FDI and ODA.
Remittances to Sub-Saharan Africa were estimated at $56 billion in 2024, up 2.4%.
FDI to Africa as a whole hit a record $97 billion in 2024, but the jump was largely one project-finance deal in Egypt; without it, FDI rose 12% to about $62 billion.

OECD preliminary data put net bilateral ODA from DAC members at $42 billion to Africa in 2024 (down 1% in real terms) and $36 billion to Sub-Saharan Africa (down 2%); this excludes aid channelled through multilateral bodies.
The OECD projected in June 2025 that bilateral ODA to Sub-Saharan Africa could fall by 16% to 28% in 2025, after a 2% fall in 2024.

In 2025, 491,950 non-EU citizens were ordered to leave the EU and 135,460 were returned to a third country after an order to leave (the two figures do not refer to the same people); Algerians (45,725) and Moroccans (29,030) received the most orders to leave.
No African nationality was among the five most returned in 2025: the largest groups returned were citizens of Türkiye, Georgia, Syria, Albania and Russia.

One research position (Clemens, 2014) holds that emigration generally rises with economic development until countries reach upper-middle income, contrary to the idea, popular in aid and trade policy, that rising incomes in poor countries deter emigration.

Another position (Lanati and Thiele, 2018; 25 donors, 129 recipients, 2004-2014) finds aid that improves public services is associated with lower emigration, but estimates that aid would have to double to cut emigration rates by only 10-15%.

gaps: Page numbers were read from the page markers in the digitised text of the two books; where a marker was missing they are given as a range.

No readable source gives the EU-wide number or share of African-born residents: Eurostat's migr_pop3ctb has an 'Africa' country-of-birth code, but the EU-27 aggregate is empty in the API, and the Statistics Explained page needs JavaScript (the PDF version has no Africa breakdown). The figure of about 9 million (2%) circulates from the Martens Centre, a party-affiliated foundation, so it was not used.

IOM World Migration Report 2024 (publications.iom.int and worldmigrationreport.iom.int) returned 403, so its Africa chapter figures (e.g. 11 million in Europe, 2020) could not be verified directly; SWP and the IOM-AU Africa Migration Report (hosted on au.int) were used instead.

UNHCR country-level host figures for Ethiopia, Sudan, DR Congo, Kenya and Egypt at end-2025 are only in annex tables/Refugee Data Finder (JavaScript, and unhcr.org returns 403); the Global Trends text gives only Uganda and Chad among African hosts.
The IMF Working Paper 2024/097 estimate (17.8 million African migrants in Africa, 2020) could not be verified (403).

UNHCR.org, UNDP.org and OCHA/ReliefWeb pages returned 403 to the checker, so the UNHCR Global Report 2025 Sudan figures (12.8 million displaced at end 2025) and the original UNDP Scaling Fences report could not be quoted directly (used UN press release, IOM newsroom and EMN Belgium summary instead)

EU recognition rates for Nigerians, Guineans, Ivorians, Senegalese, Congolese (DR) and Gambians: EUAA's per-nationality figures sit in JavaScript dashboards; only qualitative mentions (Nigerians among low-rate groups) were readable
No readable source with a Somalia EU-wide recognition rate for 2025 (only country ranges)
Number of African states criminalising same-sex relations (ILGA World) and figures on how many LGBTQ people have fled Uganda were not verified

IOM Missing Migrants Project pages and IOM/UNHCR press releases returned 403, so death figures come from Frontex and press reports that cite IOM. IOM's own regional releases give different 2025 Mediterranean totals (2,108 and 2,185 in search snippets, unverified) from the 1,878 that Frontex cites. Earlier years (2014-2022) of the Mediterranean deaths series are missing.

Frontex's 2025 release gives no per-route numbers, so 2025 route figures are proportional only (Central Mediterranean roughly flat, Western Africa about -2/3). The 2025 Central Mediterranean figure (~66,300) and the Western Mediterranean annual figures could not be verified.
The Spanish Interior Ministry's year-end PDF is behind Cloudflare, so Spanish figures come from AFP. The 2024 Canary Islands figure of 46,843 was not verified (Frontex gives 'almost 47,000').
No readable IOM source was found for deaths specifically on the Sahara crossing after May 2024.
IMF analysis (WEO April 2020 ch. 4 on the macroeconomic effects of migration) could not be verified: imf.org returned 403.

No Banca d'Italia figure on recent immigrant employment by sector, and no ISTAT primary table on foreign workers' share of employment by sector (agriculture, domestic and care work) was verified; the sector series is Fondazione Leone Moressa's value-added share on ISTAT data, not employment share.
Share of foreigners among domestic and care workers (INPS Osservatorio lavoro domestico) not verified.
No ILO primary publication on caporalato verified (ILO pages not fetched; ILO role cited via the European Labour Authority fiche).

Eurostat has no 'Africa' aggregate for first residence permits (migr_resfirst). Summing the 54 African citizenships from the Eurostat API gives about 751,000 first permits to African citizens in the EU-27 in 2025 (family 262,000; other 193,000; employment 148,000; education 148,000) and 671,000 in 2024. This is my own calculation from https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/api/dissemination/statistics/1.0/data/migr_resfirst, not a quoted figure, so it is NOT recorded as a fact; it needs to be checked or charted per country.
No readable Frontex breakdown of irregular crossings by African nationality for 2025 (the full-year release lists only the top 3: Bangladeshis, Egyptians, Afghans).

Total ODA to Sub-Saharan Africa including multilateral channels (OECD final 2024 data, reported as $66.5 billion) could not be checked: OECD pages return 403. The verified ODA figure is bilateral DAC ODA only, so it understates total aid. Note: the World Bank's Figure A.6.1 (MDB 40) appears to show total ODA to Sub-Saharan Africa at or above remittances, which goes against the common claim that remittances exceed aid for the region.
Remittances for all of Africa (Sub-Saharan Africa plus North Africa) as one figure: the World Bank's MENA region includes non-African countries, so I found no verified figure for the whole continent.
